newsitem.title: KENYA: Rights report says Kenyan justice has collapsed.
newsitem.headline: Rights report says Kenyan justice has collapsed.

text.p: Justice in Kenya has collapsed and money and power prevail in a "shadow" system of injustice fuelling mob violence, a human rights report said on Thursday.
In "Kenya Shadow Justice", the London-based African Rights group looked beyond heavily publicised political cases to what it saw as a lack of justice for ordinary Kenyans.

"The judicial system as a whole has collapsed, corrupted from within and frustrated by government interests, policies and negligence...Beyond a shortage of funds, the justice system ...faces a crisis of politics and morality," the report said.
It said claims that justice was high on the agenda for foreign donors were a facade. "In reality, Kenyan justice is corrupt and abusive; its machinery and ethos have collapsed," the report said.
"The average man and woman live in fear of it from the routine violence of the police through the corruption and inefficiency of the courts to the congested prisons," it said.

"Most Kenyan citizens are essentially victims of a system with which they have no pro-active relationship; they suffer apathy, obstruction, torture and humiliation at the hands of police, inhuman delays in remand, impoverishment and extortion."
The report, based on testimonies, documents and court sessions, detailed the sort of human rights abuses the government says it is addressing after complaints from donors and rights groups.
Other cases ranged from horrific torture to the fate of many accused people in rural areas, picked up in roundups by corrupt police seeking bribes.

It said authorities in the East African country increasingly charged opposition political activists with robbery with violence so they could then be held for long periods under threat of a death sentence.
It cited the case of Jacqueline Wangui Ngujuna who was arrested at her home with her husband, elderly uncle and teenage daughter and accused of possession of firearms in August 1992.

A search found nothing but Jacqueline and her daughter were beaten and tortured by police for two days and remanded in foul conditions for three months. She then had to go to court every two weeks for mention of her case for a total of two years.
It said overcrowded prisons were "a dumping ground for the human debris of a collapsed judicial system" and the government released no information on executions.
The London-based group said foreign donors were reluctant to condemn the government, saying they believed there was no specific policy of rights abuses despite their prevalence.

"This is dangerous and short-sighted...A government that takes little action after it is is made aware by national newspapers, on a daily basis, of routine violence in its police and security forces is absolutely culpable," the report said.
The 266-page report said foreign donors might pay for police training but officers remained licensed to commit abuses by a political framework controlled by President Daniel arap Moi.
Moi, in power since 1978, will seek re-election next year.
It said the judicial system was exploited by the government to impede political change while land rights were disputed across Kenya with the government playing on legal confusion.
